The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(N=2100\). For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(n)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(n\).

In one move, replacing \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) replaces the two \(p\)-exponents by their minimum and maximum. Thus, for each prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-exponents on the board is invariant.

At the stopping moment, no move changes the board. This means every pair of numbers on the board is comparable by divisibility. Sorting the final board as \(b_1\le b_2\le \cdots \le b_N\), we have \(b_i\mid b_{i+1}\) for all \(i\). Hence for each prime \(p\), the sequence \(v_p(b_1),\dots,v_p(b_N)\) is nondecreasing. Since its multiset is the same as the multiset of \(p\)-exponents among \(1,2,\dots,2100\), the \(k\)-th term must be the \(k\)-th smallest \(p\)-exponent in the original list.

We need the 2026th smallest \(p\)-exponent among \(1,\dots,2100\). For a fixed prime \(p\), exactly \(\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^r}\right\rfloor\) numbers have \(p\)-exponent at least \(r\). Let the 2026th smallest exponent be \(e\). Then at most \(2100-2026=74\) numbers have exponent at least \(e+1\), so

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^{e+1}}\right\rfloor \le 74.
\]

Since \(\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{m}\right\rfloor \le 74\) exactly when \(m>28\), this means

\[
p^{e+1}>28 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^e\le 28.
\]

Thus \(e\) is the largest integer with \(p^e\le 28\). Now:

- \(p=2\): \(2^4=16\le 28<32\), so \(e=4\).
- \(p=3\): \(3^3=27\le 28<81\), so \(e=3\).
- \(p=5\): \(5^2=25\le 28<125\), so \(e=2\).
- \(p=7,11,13,17,19,23\): each has \(p^1\le 28<p^2\), so \(e=1\).
- For all primes \(p\ge 29\), \(e=0\).

Therefore the 2026th smallest final number is

\[
2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Its number of positive divisors is

\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 64
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
